summary: This best current practice document gives guidelines for writing definitions of new IPFIX Information Elements. It explains the conventions for elements registered with IANA and gives guidance to expert reviewers evaluating registrations.

plainLanguage.summary: IPFIX exports network measurements as named fields, and anyone can propose a new one. This document is the rulebook for writing those proposals well, and for the group of experts who read them and decide which get registered.

questions: how to define ipfix information elements
what is an ipfix information element
how to register a new ipfix information element
subtitle: The rulebook for inventing new IPFIX data fields, and for the experts who decide whether they get registered.

tldr.problem: IPFIX lets anyone add new data fields, and the registry of them is shared by everyone, so badly designed fields cost the whole community. There was no agreed rulebook for writing them or for reviewing them.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets rules for naming, choosing a data type, numbering, structuring and reviewing an Information Element, and it defines the role of the IE-DOCTORS, the group of experts appointed by the IESG who review registrations and can approve, ask for changes or refuse them.
tldr.outcome: New IPFIX fields are registered only if they are needed, reuse what already exists, look like the elements already in the registry, and carry no more internal structure than necessary. The document also says when not to register a field at all, and what to do when a registered field turns out to be wrong.

facts.label: Required parts of a definition
facts.value: A name, a data type and a description in English

today: RFC 7013 is BCP 184, a Best Current Practice from September 2013. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Document Is For
sections.content:
The document gives guidelines for defining new IPFIX Information Elements beyond those already in the IANA IPFIX Information Element Registry. Because the data export format is self-describing, defining a new Information Element is often enough to apply IPFIX to a new measurement or management use case.

It is written for two separate audiences. For those defining new Information Elements it gives specifications and best practices for deciding which elements a given application needs, instructions for writing the definitions, and information on the supporting documentation required for a new application, up to and including the publication of one or more RFCs describing it. For the IPFIX experts appointed as IE-DOCTORS, and for IANA personnel changing the registry, it defines a set of acceptance criteria against which proposed elements should be evaluated.

The document is not intended to guide the extension of the IPFIX protocol itself, such as new export mechanisms or data types; those should be pursued through Standards Track RFCs in the IPFIX Working Group. Together with RFC 7012 it defines the procedures for management of the IANA IPFIX Information Element Registry, and its practices are meant to guide experts reviewing additions or changes under the Expert Review policy of RFC 5226.

The document essentially codifies two meta-guidelines: define new Information Elements that look like existing Information Elements, and do not define Information Elements unless you need to.
sections.plainLanguage: The document tells two groups how to work. One group writes proposals for new IPFIX fields. The other group, the IE-DOCTORS, reviews them against a list of acceptance criteria. The two rules underneath everything are that a new field should look like the fields already there, and that a new field should not be written at all unless it is really needed.

sections.title: When IPFIX Is the Right Tool
sections.content:
Although IPFIX was specified for the export of IP Flow information, its message format, template mechanism and data model made it applicable to a wide variety of network management situations. Beyond flow information export and packet information export as specified by Packet Sampling, any application with the following characteristics is a good candidate for an IPFIX application.

  • The application's data flow is fundamentally unidirectional. IPFIX is a push protocol, supporting only the export of information from an exporting process to a collecting process; request and response interactions are not supported.
  • The application handles discrete event information, or information to be periodically reported. IPFIX is particularly well suited to representing events, which can be scoped in time.
  • The application handles information about network entities. The IPFIX information model is network-oriented, so network management applications have many opportunities for reuse of the information model.
  • The application requires a small number of arrangements of data structures relative to the number of records it handles. The template-driven self-description mechanism used by IPFIX excels at handling large volumes of identically structured data, compared with representations that define structure inline with the data, such as XML.

Once IPFIX has been found to be a good fit, the next step is to work out which Information Elements are needed to represent the information the application requires. Especially for network-centric applications the IANA registry may already contain everything needed, in which case no work inside the IETF is necessary: define templates and start exporting. Most applications will be able to reuse some existing elements, but may need to define some additional ones.
sections.plainLanguage: IPFIX was built for flow data, but it works for much more. It suits applications where data only flows one way, where events happen at a point in time, where the subject is a piece of the network, and where many records share the same shape. Once that fits, the next question is which fields to use.

sections.title: Naming, Data Types and Numbers
sections.content:
An Information Element is eligible for inclusion in the IANA registry if it is unique within the registry and its description represents a substantially different meaning from any existing element, if it contains as little internal structure as possible, and if it does not describe a proprietary or nonstandard application, which should use enterprise-specific elements instead. Defining one requires a descriptive name, a data type from the IPFIX Data Type subregistry, and a human-readable description written in English.

On naming: the name is the first thing a potential implementor will use to judge suitability, so it should be as precise and descriptive as possible. Names must be unique within the registry, start with lowercase letters, and use capital letters for the first letter of each component except the first, with all other letters lowercase even for acronyms. Exceptions are made for acronyms that mix cases, such as IPv4 and IPv6, so sourceMacAddress and destinationIPv4Address are correct. An element pertaining to a specific protocol should name that protocol in the first word, such as sipMethod, and one pertaining to a specific application should name the application in the first word.

On data types: the most appropriate type should be chosen from the informationElementDataTypes subregistry. An element representing an integral value with a natural width should use the matching integral type, especially for values taken directly from fixed-width fields in a measured protocol, so tcpControlBits is an unsigned8 and tcpSequenceNumber is an unsigned32. Counters and identifiers should be signed64 or unsigned64 as appropriate to maximise the range of values, with reduced-size encoding used where fewer values are needed. Time values must be given the appropriate precision, so a value measured at second-level precision uses dateTimeSeconds rather than dateTimeMilliseconds. Strings and octetArrays with length constraints must state those constraints in their description. The type must match the data it represents, so information that could be a string but better matches another type must use that type even if the source represented it differently.

On numbering: each element has a unique identifier in the registry, and IANA should assign the lowest available identifier in the range 128 to 32767. Identifiers in the range 1 to 127 are reserved for compatibility with the corresponding fields in NetFlow version 9.
sections.plainLanguage: A new field needs three things: a name, a data type and a description in English. The name starts in lower case and uses capitals for each word after the first, the data type must match the kind of value, and the number comes from the middle of the registry range because the low numbers belong to the older NetFlow format.

sections.title: Semantics, Units, Structure and Multiplicity
sections.content:
Elements to which special semantics apply should refer to a value in the Information Element Semantics subregistry, subject to the restrictions of RFC 5610, so that the semantics and the type are consistent. The units of a dimensioned quantity or an entity count should be given in the units field, taken from the Information Element Units subregistry; a unit not yet in that subregistry must be added at the same time as the element. Where the range of values an element can take is smaller than the range implied by its data type, the range should be defined in the registry entry.

Defining an element with internal structure described in its Description field is not recommended, except in four cases: the element is a direct copy of a structured entity in a measured protocol, such as the TCP flags byte; it represents a section of a packet or protocol entity in raw form as captured from the wire, such as an MPLS label stack section; it represents a set of tightly related flags that should always appear together, where separate one-byte booleans would be inefficient; or it contains internal structure by reference to an external data type or specification, such as a MIME type or a URL. Additional exceptions should be made through the publication of an RFC. In other cases a candidate element with internal structure should be decomposed into multiple primitive elements exported in parallel, or into an IPFIX Structured Data element. The example given is an endpoint, a host, port and protocol tuple, which should be represented by separate source address, source port and transport protocol elements rather than one opaque structured element. That normalisation also increases opportunities for reuse.

Multiplicity has three options. Where the items have a natural order and the multiplicity is the same for each record, several instances of the element can appear in the template. Where the multiplicity varies, a basicList of the element can be used in the IPFIX Structured Data extension. Where the structure is taken directly from bytes seen on the wire, such as a TCP options stack, it can be exported as a variable-length octetArray holding the raw content. A new element should not encode multiplicity or ordinality information into its own definition.

Where an element takes an enumerated value from a set that may change, the enumeration must be defined by an IANA registry or subregistry. An existing registry that defines the enumeration must be used, as with the IANA Protocol Numbers registry for protocolIdentifier; otherwise a new subregistry of the IANA IPFIX registry must be defined for it. Finally, new elements that cannot be reversed for bidirectional flow export must say so in their description.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules push towards simple fields. A field should not carry a hidden structure of its own unless it is a straight copy of something on the wire, and any structure should be split into separate fields that can be reused elsewhere. How many items a record holds is a property of the record, not of the field.

sections.title: The Life Cycle: Review, Revision and Deprecation
sections.content:
Once the elements for an application have been identified, their specifications are submitted to IANA, which forwards the request to the IE-DOCTORS, the experts appointed by the IESG under the Expert Review policy. The IE-DOCTORS review the request for compliance with this document, with other applicable IPFIX-related RFCs, and for consistency with the elements already defined. Authors are expected to check their own submissions against the document first. If the request is acceptable the IE-DOCTORS signal approval to IANA, which changes the registry; if it is not, they can work with the requester to make it compliant, and may in exceptional circumstances reject a clearly frivolous request outright. This process does not allow the IE-DOCTORS to overrule IETF consensus: elements that were added with IETF consensus require IETF consensus to revise or deprecate. Decisions may be appealed as in Section 7 of RFC 5226.

Revising an element starts by sending a new definition to IANA. The primary requirement is the avoidance of interoperability problems, and changes to elements already in use may only be made in an interoperable way; a necessary change that cannot be made interoperably must result in deprecation instead. A change is interoperable when it corrects an obviously editorial error, corrects an ambiguity severe enough to prevent the element being used as originally defined, expands the data type without changing how the value is represented, corrects missing information without changing the meaning, defines a previously undefined or reserved enumerated value or reserved flag bit, expands the set of permissible values in the range, or harmonizes with an external reference that was itself corrected. Each element carries a revision number starting at zero, each accepted change increments it, and the date of the most recent revision is recorded. The registry does not need to keep old revisions, since every revision had to be interoperable.

Deprecation applies when a definition has an error or shortcoming that cannot be permissibly changed, when the deprecation harmonizes with an external reference that was itself deprecated, or when changes to the protocol or to community understanding allow the same information to be represented more efficiently or conveniently; the last case requires a Standards Action. The description in the registry must be updated to explain the deprecation and to refer to any replacement elements, and the revision number is incremented. Deprecated elements should continue to be supported by collecting processes but should not be exported by exporting processes, and their use should produce a log entry or human-readable warning. Names and element identifiers of deprecated elements must not be reused.
sections.plainLanguage: A new field is submitted to IANA and handed to a group of experts, who check it against these rules and either accept it, ask for changes, or refuse it. Once registered, a field may only be changed in ways that keep old and new implementations working together; anything else means the field is deprecated, with a replacement named in its description.

sections.title: When Not to Define New Information Elements
sections.content:
Because the number space of Information Elements in the registry is limited and the difficulty of managing and understanding the registry grows with its size, avoiding redundancy and clutter matters. New elements should not be added to the IANA registry unless there is an intent to implement and deploy applications using them; research or experimental applications should use enterprise-specific elements instead.

New applications should prefer existing elements wherever possible. IPFIX already provides elements for every common Layer 4 and Layer 3 packet header field in the IETF protocol suite, for basic Layer 2 information, for basic counters, for timestamps and for time ranges. Reviewers should make sure an existing element is not applicable before accepting a similar new one. This does not mean an element that represents the same information from a packet as an existing element cannot be added: ipClassOfService, ipDiffServCodePoint and ipPrecedence all represent subsets of the same field in an IPv4 header but different uses of those bits, and which one is used says how the bits were interpreted. Changing the context in which an element is used is on the other hand not enough reason for a new one, so an extension that logs HTTP transactions alongside network information should reuse sourceIPv4Address and destinationIPv4Address rather than define httpClientAddress and httpServerAddress.

Applications dealing with bidirectional interactions should use the bidirectional flow support of RFC 5103. Existing timestamp and time range elements should be reused for any simple time stamping of an event: the observationTime elements from Packet Sampling for single observations, and the flowStart and flowEnd elements for events with a duration. New timestamp elements should only be defined for semantically distinct timing information, such as a record describing an event scheduled in the future. The use of absolute timestamp elements is recommended. Timestamps relative to the export time of the enclosing message may be used when high precision matters and bandwidth or storage is limited, and timestamps relative to a separately exported options record may be used only where the application already uses runtime-defined epochs; new applications should avoid these structures where possible.

Enterprise-specific elements are scoped to a vendor's or organisation's Private Enterprise Number and are under the complete control of the assigning organisation. They are the right answer for implementation-specific information, for research or experiments within a single organisation or closed community, for information derived in a commercially sensitive or proprietary way, and for information specific to a proprietary application. They are also useful for pre-standardisation testing of a new application: while a new application is being developed and interoperability tested, the elements it uses should not be submitted to IANA but represented as enterprise-specific until their definitions are finalised. Organisations using enterprise-specific elements are advised to follow the same guidelines.
sections.plainLanguage: Most new fields are not needed. The registry already covers the common header fields, counters and timestamps, and reusing them keeps the registry small. A new field belongs in the IANA registry only when someone intends to build and run a product with it; anything else, including experiments, belongs in the enterprise-specific space where one organisation controls it.

sections.title: The IESpec Textual Format
sections.content:
Example templates in existing IPFIX documents are usually given as bitmap diagrams of the wire representation. These illustrate simple templates but are not readable for complicated ones, give no support for rapid implementation, and do not convey that ordering and extra elements are optional. The document therefore defines a recommended textual format for specifying elements and templates in Internet-Drafts, with human readability, human writability, compactness and ease of parser implementation as design goals, without needing external XML support.

The basis is the textual Information Element Specifier, or IESpec, which carries the four important aspects of an element: its name, its number, its type and its size. Bare words are names, parentheses hold numbers, angle brackets hold data types, square brackets hold sizes, and curly braces hold an optional space-separated list of context identifiers. The symbol + is reserved for elements nested inside structured data elements. Whitespace is insignificant.

The fully qualified form for an IANA-registered element is name(number)<type>[size], where the size is the length in octets, with 65535 or the string v signifying a variable-length element; the size may be omitted, in which case the data type's native or default size is assumed. For an enterprise-specific element the form is name(pen/number)<type>[size]. A partial IESpec is any specifier that is not fully qualified, and takes missing values from the canonical definition in the registry; at minimum it must contain a name or a number, and size information in a partial specifier overrides the size in the registry, which is how reduced-size encoding is expressed.

A template is an ordered, newline-separated sequence of IESpecs, and Flow Keys may be annotated by appending the {key} context. An Options Template is specified similarly, with the {scope} context appended to each scope element, and all scope elements must appear before any non-scope element. IESpecs can also describe the IPFIX Structured Data extension, where the elements inside a structured data element follow it and are prefixed with +, with more plus signs for deeper nesting.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives a compact text form for writing down IPFIX fields: the name in plain text, the number in parentheses, the type in angle brackets and the size in square brackets. A template is then just one such line per field, which is easier to read and to write than a diagram of the bytes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The IE-DOCTORS must evaluate the security aspects of new Information Elements in light of the information they could provide to support attacks against the measured network or against the entities about which information is exported. The aspects to evaluate include whether the exported information contains personally identifiable information, or information that should be kept confidential about the described entities, such as partial payload or configuration information that could be exploited.

This is not a reason not to define such elements; there must be an evaluation of the security risk against the utility of the exported information for the intended application. The example given is the framework for packet selection and reporting, which concluded that the private parameters of the hash function should not be exported within IPFIX. Security considerations specific to an element must be addressed in the Security Considerations section of the Internet-Draft describing it, or in the element's own description when it is not defined in an Internet-Draft, and elements with specific security considerations should be described in an Internet-Draft. The ipHeaderPacketSection element is given as an example, noting that with sufficient length it also reports octets from the IP payload, subject to the IETF policy on wiretapping. Packet Sampling is given as another, saying a device should not export the full payload of conversations and must respect local privacy laws.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new field is checked for what it might reveal. If a field would expose personal data or confidential detail about the network being measured, the experts weigh that against the use the field has, and the definition must say what the exposure is.

viz.caption: The two rules the document reduces to

items.title: Look like the existing elements
items.text: A new Information Element should look like the ones already in the registry, so that implementors and collectors can handle it the same way.

items.title: Do not define one unless you need to
items.text: The registry has a limited number space, and the difficulty of managing and understanding it grows with its size.

items.title: Reuse before you define
items.text: IPFIX already has elements for the common header fields, counters, timestamps and time ranges.

items.title: The IE-DOCTORS review
items.text: Experts appointed by the IESG check each proposal against these rules and the other IPFIX documents, and can approve it, ask for changes or refuse it.

viz.caption: Four signs that an application fits IPFIX

items.title: The data only flows one way
items.text: IPFIX is a push protocol, supporting only export from an exporting process to a collecting process.

items.title: It handles events
items.text: Discrete event information, or information reported periodically, is particularly well suited to IPFIX.

items.title: It is about network entities
items.text: The information model is network-oriented, so network management applications have many opportunities for reuse.

items.title: Many records, few shapes
items.text: The template-driven self-description mechanism handles large volumes of identically structured data well.

cells: An integral value with a natural width
The matching integral type, so tcpControlBits is an unsigned8 and tcpSequenceNumber is an unsigned32.
A counter or an identifier
signed64 or unsigned64 to maximise the range, with reduced-size encoding where fewer values are needed.
A time value
The type with the right precision, so a second-level measurement uses dateTimeSeconds.
An address
An address type, even when the source system held the address as a string.
A value from a set that may grow
An enumerated type taken from an existing registry, or from a new IANA subregistry created for it.

viz.caption: The only four cases where a field may carry its own structure

items.title: A straight copy from a measured protocol
items.text: Such as the TCP flags byte, exported as tcpControlBits.

items.title: Raw bytes from the wire
items.text: Such as a section of an MPLS label stack, exported in the form it was captured.

items.title: Tightly related flags
items.text: A set of flags that always appear together, where separate one-byte booleans would be inefficient.

items.title: A reference to an external specification
items.text: Internal structure by reference to an external data type or specification, such as a MIME type or a URL.

viz.caption: The changes that keep old and new implementations working together

cells: An obviously editorial correction
A typo in the definition.
A correction of an ambiguity
One severe enough to stop the element being used as originally defined, as with a prior change to ipv6ExtensionHeaders.
A wider data type, same representation
Changing unsigned32 to unsigned64, as with a prior change to selectorId.
Missing information, same meaning
Defining the quantity semantics for numeric elements that had no data type semantics.
A newly defined enumerated value or flag bit
Defining a value or a reserved bit that was previously undefined.
A wider range of values
Expanding the set of permissible values in the element's range.
Harmonising with a corrected reference
Following a change to an external specification that was itself corrected.
